All 12 D items are in it, matched to codes by wording: D1-D6 = .s002 items 1-6, D9 = 7, D7 = 9, D10-D12 = 10-12, D8 = 13 (listed under the 'Attitude on Dengue Prevention' heading there; .s002 item 8 is E6). 9/12 are character-identical to Table 2; three differ trivially and .s002 is shipped: D1 has a final period (Table 2 lacks it), D3 reads 'So, I am not' (Table 2 'So I am not'), D9 has a straight apostrophe in I'm (Table 2 curly). Leading numbering and cell whitespace stripped. REVERSE-SCORED STORAGE (important): the live table stores D2, D3, D7, D8, D9, D10, D11, D12 reverse-scored (live = 9 - administered response) and D1, D4, D5, D6 as administered. Evidence: (i) Table 2's printed raw means reflect onto the live means for those eight at the same SD -- e.g. D8 printed 7.34 (1.29), live 1.6561 (1.2896) = 9 - 7.344; D7 6.63 (1.51) vs live 2.3715 (1.5054); D10 2.25 (1.56) vs 6.7549 (1.5620) -- while D1/D4/D5/D6 match unreflected (D4 7.87 (0.58) vs 7.8696 (0.5797)); (ii) the authors' own S1 Data Sheet3 (test-retest sheet, header only, no values) carries paired columns D2_r, D3_r, D7_r, D8_r, D9_r, D10_r, D11_r, D12_r -- exactly this eight; (iii) read raw, D8 ('With at least one person who is knowledgeable ... can help prevent the disease') would sit at 1.66/8, implausible beside the attitude items' 6.1-7.8. The paper itself never states reverse scoring. So, as for burkert_2019_whoqol_bref / baka2023_bpnsf, anchors are shipped to match the stored direction: for the eight reversed items resp 1 = 'Strongly Agree' and resp 8 = 'Strongly Disagree'; for D1, D4, D5, D6 resp 1 = 'Strongly Disagree', resp 8 = 'Strongly Agree'. Direction for D12 is the weakest (near-uniform distribution; live 4.4229 -> 4.577 reflected vs printed 4.56, 0.017 off, vs 0.137 off unreflected) and rests mainly on the D12_r header. This is also a response-table caveat: nothing in the IRW response table flags that 8 of 12 items are stored reversed. OPTIONS: paper Methods: 8-point scale '1 = strongly disagree ... 8 = strongly agree'; .s002 prints 'Strongly / Disagree' under 1 and 'Strongly / Agree' under 8 (joined, .s002 capitalisation). resp 2-7 option_text blank (no labels exist in any source; not padded). LANGUAGE: paper says the RPAP was 'bilingual in both English and Malay' (developed in English); Malay wording is in neither the article, .s002 (English only) nor .s001 (item headers are bare codes; Malay only in demographic headers), so language='English; Malay', English base fields, no _translated columns. (1) CODE DERIVATION: number-preserving rename -- the script renames caug<i>pre/caug<i>post to caug<i> (wave 1/2); no positional step. (2) LEVEL-1 CHECK: the .sav was opened; its caug variable labels carry no wording (caug1pre 'test CAUGpre', caug1post 'CAUG POST', the rest unlabelled); value labels on all 20 columns are 1 incorrecto / 2 apenas cierto / 3 mas bien cierto / 4 cierto, matching the script's MAP_CAUG. So the item wording comes from the study's codebook S2, which prints each item against the data's own code CAUG1..CAUG10 (paper_explicit). (3) ADMINISTERED LANGUAGE: Spanish (Universidad Rey Juan Carlos, Madrid; paper says 'the Spanish version of the ten-item General Self-Efficacy Scale'). item_text = the codebook's 'Item in Spanish' column verbatim (only a trailing space on CAUG10 stripped); option_text = the codebook's 'Scale in Spanish' anchors ('Incorrecto','Apenas cierto','Mas bien cierto','Cierto', unaccented 'Mas' kept verbatim; the .sav value labels are the same words in lowercase). (4) ENGLISH (_translated): item_text_translated is the study's own English from article Table 4, assigned to each code by matching content to the Spanish item (the Spanish GSE is a reordered translation: CAUG1 = English 'If someone opposes me', CAUG2 = 'solve difficult problems if I try hard enough', ..., CAUG7 = 'No matter what comes my way', CAUG10 = 'several solutions'). Table 4 lists items in canonical English order and ties none to a code, so it was not used for the mapping. The codebook's own 'Item in English' column agrees in content with Table 4 for 8/10 codes but prints CAUG2 = 'I can solve most problems if I invest the necessary effort' and CAUG8 = 'I can always manage to solve difficult problems if I try hard enough' -- the reverse of its own Spanish column for those two rows. The Spanish column was followed because it is what respondents read and it reproduces the published Spanish GSE order (item 2 'Puedo resolver problemas dificiles si me esfuerzo lo suficiente', item 8 'Puedo resolver la mayoria de los problemas si me esfuerzo lo necesario'). The codebook's English column also has typos ('find he means', 'rely on m coping') that Table 4 does not; Table 4 wording was preferred throughout. option_text_translated = codebook 'Scale in English' (Not at all true / Hardly true / Moderately true / Exactly true). No instructions text exists in the paper or codebook for this block; left blank. (5) STEP 3b: live data are 10 items, resp 1-4, matching the 10-item 4-point GSE; not a mismatch. The codebook attributes the scale to 'Gonzales, N. (2013) ... Unpublished manuscript' and asks 'What does CAUG mean?'; the items are nonetheless the Spanish GSE, which the paper cites as Schwarzer & Jerusalem 1995 [66]. (6) VERIFICATION: see verification row -- live per-item x level counts equal the .sav columns cell for cell (20/20, both waves), and the GSE item-mean reproduces Table 5 within 0.007 in all four group x wave cells. Data cannot separate caug2 from caug8 (pre means 3.437 vs 3.419, near-synonymous items), so that pair rests on the codebook's Spanish column. (7) RIGHTS: not a block. Schwarzer & Jerusalem's GSE FAQ (faq_gse.pdf, sha256 above) states: 'We hereby grant you permission to use and reproduce the General Self-Efficacy Scale for your study, given that appropriate recognition of the source of the scale is made in the write-up of your study.' Attribution only; no fee/NC/ND/no-redistribution clause. Consistent with batch_239 (ye_2025_q25_scale) and santos_2018_gse. Per the 2026-09-10 rule no instrument_rights_register.csv ship row was written; escalated as a ship-shaped case.
